turn_text: Many people are trying to understand what the relationship might between China and the US might look like in the future. Do you have any thoughts for how to make that the most productive possible relationship?

I think China is intent on replacing us, conquering us militarily, economically and geopolitically. I don't think necessarily through a war, but I think they would want to have, if you will, the dominant power, certainly in the Pacific and ultimately in the world. militarily, as well as economically and geopolitically. They plan to replace us. We have been the, if you will, the superpower, the hyper-power, all in the collapse of the Iron Curtain, and they want to assume that position. I think they would look for an authoritarian world where they basically dictate to the world what the conditions are for economic trade and the like. And so that's a pretty frightening objective on their part. And my view is that the nations of the rest of the world, the West Democratic nations, nations that follow the rule of law, that those nations need to come together and say, wait a second, what are the rules going to be that we're going to live by? And we would have to deny to China the right to have access to our markets so they don't play by those rules. And it is my hope that if we're successful in doing that as a group of ourselves coming together and developing those rules that the China would be dissuaded from a course of confrontation and instead play a more collaborative, competitive role in the geopolitical marketplace.

turn_text: Many admired your statement on Trump's impeachment. When do you know when to stand with the team and when to be uncompromising in your values?

It's pretty straightforward in a setting like impeachment where having already sworn an oath to defend the Constitution as a Senator, we were required to swear an additional oath when the impeachment trial occurred. And the Chief Justice of the United States in the first case, and then the President Pro Tem in the second case administered a new oath of office where we swore to apply impartial justice, so help us God. And at that point, when you swear to apply impartial justice, that suggests that you're not going to be partial to a team or a party or even a personal relationship. It's impartial. And you're going to try and do what is in your judgment, the right thing. So for me, that's pretty straightforward that in a circumstance like that you are you're swearing before God to put Your your conscience and which you think is right above all above all else There are other circumstances where where you say let's say in a policy matter, which is that should we adjust a a tax for instance You say okay, you know, I don't like that tax, but I do like what our our group of people is doing generally So I'm gonna work with them on this one and help them on this, but even though I don't like it very much, it's not a matter of principle, I just don't like it much. And because I think in the long run, we can work together on something I like better. I mean, that's the nature of saying, how do you get things done that conforms with what your view would be? I mean, you don't want to be oppositional on everything that you have any disagreement with. There are some people, by the way, that want to fight every single thing they don't agree with 100%. They don't get much done. So I'd like to say, could I agree with elements in a proposal? If I do, and if our group wants to do it, and I think that our group or our party has some prospects that will be better for the American people, that's something I'm going to consider.

turn_text: Senator, thank you so much for your time. We'd like to, for a final question, I'd love to know, as you think about your career, we'd love to hear a little bit about perhaps what you're most proud of, or anything you might do differently. Maybe to borrow the question from Clayton Christensen, who you mentioned. How do you think about measuring your life?

The most important thing in my life is my relationship to God and my relationship with my wife. The form of my relationship with my Father in Heaven takes work and that means prayer and it means service and scripture study and some of those things I do better than others. the relationship that's also critical to me, my relationship with my wife, has frankly been extraordinarily natural. I would rather be with Anne than any other person or do, or any other thing. I mean, there's nothing I'd rather be or do than be with my wife. And that just comes naturally. So I'm with her as much of the time as I can possibly be. I know for other people marriage is a more studied effort. And so I salute those. My relationship with my wife is very, very good. Next, my relationship with my kids is most important. And I'm really pleased that I love my kids. My kids love me. I have 25 grandkids. I love them dearly. I believe they love me as well. And so, frankly, how I measure my life is associated with my relationship with my father in heaven, with my wife and family, and with my friends. And finally, I do have a number of really good friends. I make an effort to connect with them as often as I can, not as much as I'd like. But that's really if you look at my personal balance sheet, those are the big assets. The career I've had, I just want to be able to say that I did my best, that I followed my conscience, that I didn't do things that I felt were dishonorable or untruthful. And as long as I feel good about those things, I feel great. Frankly, success, there's no question. I can't escape the fact that that being successful in business and in politics makes you feel good. There's no question about that. That's just the nature of the society we live in. But as I step back and look at my life, and I think about what it's going to be like when I have a terminal disease or what I getting prepared to meet my maker, The successes I've had in business or in financial matters or in politics will pale in comparison with those other items that I mentioned first.
